As we will see from Phenomenology itself, phenomena really do depend on one another. Together they form a single unbroken chain of theses, antitheses, and syntheses.

The exposition of Phenomenology therefore follows exactly the same chain. It follows it so closely that one might easily get the impression that this dialectical elegance belongs to the exposition itself—that it is the result of some special “method” of investigation and presentation.
But we have seen that this is not the case.
The dialectical character of phenomenological description comes from the object being described.

And we have also seen that because of the nature of this object, phenomenological description—as a “phenomenological method,” if we want to call it that—is necessarily dialectical in another sense: in explaining the description, we must also explain something about the “objective” dialectic itself, which exists independently of the description.
So let us ask: what is this objective dialectic discovered by Hegel, studied since then by Marxism-Leninism-Stalinism, and now to be described phenomenologically in this book?

We know that dialectic belongs first of all not to discourse about the world, but to the existing world itself. It is a real and fundamental quality of that world—or, if you prefer, the general and real form of its existence.

We can also say that dialectic is the fundamental law governing the relations between the elements that make up the world. It unites them in space into a single whole and determines their mutual dependence through time.
If dialectic is the real form of the world’s existence, then the world’s existence is simply the realization—or “materialization”—of this dialectical form in space and time.
The spatio-temporal world no more exists apart from dialectic than dialectic exists apart from the world.
This is how Hegel speaks about dialectic, or something close to it.
But if we want his claim to be fully accurate, we need to make one essential correction.
When Hegel spoke about dialectic, he spoke about the world in general: the natural world as well as the human world.
What I have just said becomes completely correct only if we add the adjective “human” every time we use the word “world.”
Dialectic is the real form of existence of the human world, not of the natural world.
It is therefore the human world, not the natural world, that realizes dialectic in space and time.
The natural world exists without dialectic. Dialectic, however, does not exist without the human world.

In other words, the human world is ultimately nothing other than the realization of dialectic within the spatio-temporal, material world of nature. Conversely, real dialectic is nothing other than this human world taken across the whole of its existence in space and time.
We might therefore compare the natural world to a non-dialectical canvas on which the dialectical picture called the universal history of humanity is painted.
A painting cannot exist without a canvas. In the same way, the human world—and therefore dialectic—cannot exist without the natural world or outside it.
Yet a painting, provided it is more than a random mixture of colours and is genuinely a work of art, differs essentially and radically from the canvas on which it is painted.
In the same way, the human world—that is, real dialectic—differs essentially and radically from the non-dialectical natural world.
Strictly speaking, it would be even better to identify the natural world not only with the canvas but also with the paints and the other materials used to make the picture.

A painting is, if you like, nothing but these paints and materials. Its weight, its physical dimensions, and its duration in time are simply the weight, dimensions, and duration of those materials. Nothing is physically “added” to them.
And yet the painting is also “something else.”

The paints themselves have a particular chemical composition. But the painting as a work of art—the “something” that makes it exceptional, ordinary, or mediocre—has neither weight nor chemical composition.
Yet this “something” exists in some sense. An exceptional painting differs from a mediocre one just as “really” as an oil painting differs from a watercolour.

The human world as a whole stands in relation to the natural world in exactly the same way. It is like the “aesthetic” something—the elusive quality that makes the painting what it is—in relation to the physical material, with all its weight, from which the painting is made.
First of all, the human being is “nothing” apart from their natural, animal body.
There is no “soul” independent of the body that somehow gets added to it from outside.
If the body dies, the human being disappears with it, just as a painting would disappear if it were destroyed in a fire.
Yet any impartial observer can see that a human being differs essentially and radically from an animal. A human being is not only a body but also “something else.”

The specifically human difference between “heroes” and “bastards,” for example, is just as great and just as “real” as the difference between someone fat and someone thin, or someone blond and someone dark-haired—even though this “ethical” something is every bit as elusive as the painting’s “aesthetic” something.
A human being is nothing outside the natural world. Yet within the natural world, a human being is “something else” from all the purely natural “things” around them.
And human beings are dialectical precisely because they are not merely natural “things” but also “something other,” even though this “something” is, in itself, “nothing.”
Dialectic is nothing other than this “nothing” which, within the natural world, has become the “something other” we call the human being.
Someone explains how to make a doughnut with a hole in it:
“You take a hole,” they say, “and wrap some dough around it.”
If this person were a philosopher, they would belong to the “idealist” or “spiritualist” camp. They would say that to make a human being, you take a “soul” and “wrap” a body around it.
But as we now know, this “theory” of the human being is just as absurd as the joke’s recipe for a doughnut.
There is no soul outside the body or before the body, just as there is no hole before the doughnut.
But it does not follow that the hole does not exist—that there is no hole in a ring doughnut.
That, however, is effectively what vulgar “materialism” claims when it says that there is no difference between a human being and any other natural “thing,” such as an animal.
There is a difference. A ring doughnut is not the same thing as a solid doughnut.

But the difference lies entirely in the “hole”—in something that does not “exist” independently, in a “nothing” that becomes “something” through the doughnut but is itself nothing apart from the ring doughnut.
You can eat the doughnut, for example, but you cannot eat the hole.
Yet without the hole, what you are eating is not a ring doughnut but a solid doughnut or something like one.
The ring doughnut therefore no more exists without the hole than the hole exists without the doughnut.
The same is true of the world.
Human beings do not exist outside the natural world, and therefore neither does dialectic. Yet the world would not be dialectical if human beings did not exist within it.
There was once a time when there were no human beings in the world.
The world was then purely natural. Nothing in it was dialectical, and dialectic did not exist at all.
In principle, we can also imagine a time when humanity will have died out completely.
The world will then cease to be dialectical and will once again become purely natural. Dialectic will disappear without leaving a trace.
In this sense, we can say that dialectic is nothing other than the human being insofar as the human being differs from animals, plants, and every other natural “thing.”
What distinguishes human beings from natural “things” is precisely this:

But if human beings do not exist outside the natural world, their existence must consist in an interaction with that world—just as the existence of the hole in a doughnut consists in its “interaction” with the doughnut.
More precisely, the human being is this interaction itself.
We cannot say that human beings exist before this interaction or independently of it.
Before it and outside it, there is nothing except the natural world. Or, if you prefer, the human being before and outside this interaction is nothing.
But once the interaction exists, this “nothing” becomes a “something,” and something other than the natural world.
That “something other” is the human being.
And because this something is other, the result of its interaction with the natural world will also be other than the natural world itself.
This “other result” is the human world.

We can say that interaction with the natural world simultaneously creates or produces both its own cause—the human being acting within nature—and its own effect or result—the human world created by human action within nature.
As cause and effect—that is, as the human being and the world created by human beings—neither exists before or outside this interaction with the natural world. They exist only through it.
This is obvious in the case of human beings themselves. Unless we believe in an “immortal,” “immaterial” soul, there simply cannot be a human being without their interaction with the natural world.
But the same is true of the world human beings create.
There is no human world without interaction with the natural world.
This human world does not merely arise from that interaction. It disappears when the interaction disappears.
Houses, machines, clothes, and so on differ from natural “things” only because human beings use them—that is, because the interaction between humanity and the natural world continues.
For a bird, for example, there is essentially no difference today between a telegraph wire on which it perches and the branch of a tree.

And if humanity disappeared, everything it had created—houses, machines, and so on—would in principle become indistinguishable from piles of stone or iron, mountains, shells, and other natural objects.
After all, these things are made from the very same “materials” that existed before human beings appeared.
A ton of steel arranged into rotary printing machinery differs essentially and radically from an ordinary ton of steel only because human beings use it to print newspapers.
Likewise, a house differs from a “natural” cave only because human beings use it as a home.
So what is dialectical first is the interaction with the non-dialectical natural world.
What is dialectical secondarily, or by derivation, is first the inseparable cause of that interaction—the human being—and then its inseparable “effect”—the human world.
We can say that human beings and the human world they create, that is, the historical world, are dialectical only because they are bound up with this interaction.
What is specifically “human” in humanity—the dialectical character of human beings and of the historical world—comes into existence with this interaction and disappears with it.

Conversely, dialectic is nothing other than this interaction taken as a whole: an interaction that includes both the human being who brings it about and the historical world that the human being produces.

For although human beings and the historical world cannot exist apart from interaction with the natural world, that interaction cannot exist apart from human beings and the historical world they create either.
To speak of interaction—that is, of dialectic—is therefore to speak of human beings and the historical world.

It is to speak of human beings insofar as they create the historical world through their interaction with the natural world, and of the historical world insofar as human beings create it through that same interaction.
In other words, to speak about dialectic is to speak about human beings insofar as they differ from animals, plants, and other natural “things.”
And it is to speak about the historical world insofar as it differs from the natural world.
So what exactly is this “historical world”?
First of all, it is the “ideal” world of human “culture”: the world of science, literature, art, religion, sport, and so on—in short, the world of what Marx called “ideological superstructures.”
At bottom, this is the world of human discourse or, more precisely, the world of the meaning carried by that discourse.
Discourse, or logos, exists only through articulated sounds—“words”—or through signs—“letters”—written on some physical surface, or finally through physico-chemical processes in a brain—“thoughts.”
Meaning physically “adds” nothing to any of these things.
Yet meaning is neither a sound, nor a sign, nor a chemical process. It is something entirely other.

And it is only the presence of this “other” that transforms sounds, signs, and chemical processes into meaningful discourse: something that exists only through human beings, in human beings, and for human beings.
Meaningful discourse is the result—or, if you prefer, one of the forms—of the dialectical interaction between human beings and the natural world.
But just as this discourse cannot exist without human beings, human beings could not exist without this discourse, and neither could the historical world they have built.
We can therefore also say that the historical world is first of all the world of human discourse—or, more exactly, the world of its meaning.
